Hey guys, as the title says, I'm an absolute beginner looking to start lifting weights and I want to go about in a way that I don't hurt myself. What should I be aware of and try to avoid in order to safely and effectively lift weights? Thanks guys!

A lot of the advice you'll get will depend on what you're going for. There's the Olympic lifting crowd, the bodybuilder crowd, the powerlifting crowd, and then the guys who just want to get a "six pack" and look good on the beach. Each is just fine, but I'm in the powerlifting clique, which revolves around competitions in the dead lift, squat, and bench press.

So, IF that's what you're into, first I have a particular book to recommend: "Starting Strength" by Mark Rippetoe. It's very well regarded in the community and will get you started on a 3 day a week program that is virtually guaranteed to work. I used it for years. There are other programs, but the best ones for beginners are all pretty similar to Rippetoe's. Included are detailed instructions of how to, and how not to do the basic lifts for maximum effect and so that you're not injured.

If you're a complete beginner, I'd like to emphasize the importance of free weights over machines. If all you did were those 3 lifts - squats, bench, DL - you'll make more progress, more quickly, than any amount of time spent on machines. For example - when I was younger, I envied guys with biceps. So I did curls. I tried everything, every variation, experimenting with different rep ranges and weights. I made only minimal progress. Then in my late twenties, with a different set of goals in mind, I started deadlifting. It was like magic - my arms and biceps started thickening up, even though I'd sworn off curls completely. Same with calves, same with forearms, etc. My point is that big lifts using multiple joints ("compound lifts") are generally regarded as the most effective for strength training and building muscle.

So, I included that above because you said you were an "absolute beginner." I'll give you a few pointers on safety.

1) Keep a rigid straight or arched back when you squat or DL. Don't let your shoulders or back slump. That's how not to hurt your back in general when you're lifting.

2) 5 minutes of cardio to warm up is good, and if it's a major lift you're doing, a few lighter warmup sets. I don't recommend stretching as part of your warmup.

3) There's a difference between the pain of burning muscles struggling against a weight they're not used to, and the pain of an injury about to happen. If it hurts and you're not sure why, stop.

4) Get enough to eat. A nutritionist would go ape shit at most of the food advice that gets passed around among lifters, but it's a simple truism that it takes a lot of food to grow your body and repair your body. And of course, the more protein, the better.
